Q: List not updating outside function scope A:

Suppose you were returning the result:

def update_list(my_list):
    my_list = my_list + [4]
    return my_list

There's no difference between that and this:

def update_list(my_list):
    result = my_list + [4]
    return result

In both cases you allocate a new local variable, and bind it to the newly constructed list of length four.

And then of course the caller would need to assign nums = update_list(nums).

In contrast, the OP code creates a new local variable and discards the result. It implicitly returns None, which isn't very useful in this context.

Your function should .append(4) if you want to have side effects on the list that was passed in.

Q: How to refactor all occurences of a string into a variable in Python with VSCode A:

I don't think VS Code has built-in support for this. I would not recommend this for pretty much anything except string literals, but a simple find-and-replace might honestly be an okay alternative.

Usually, this would be prone to false positives. If you're replacing string literals, however, any false positives would need to be bookended on both sides by quotation marks. I can't think of anything that would cause that except for nested quotes, which are pretty rare.

If you're really worried about false positives, you can always use the advanced find-and-replace menu (the magnifying glass on the left sidebar, or CTRL+SHIFT+H). This will give you a preview of every change before you hit the replace button, which lets you spot those errors beforehand.

Make sure to check for multiple quote styles, of course. Single and double quotes definitely need independent operations (unless you use a regex, which seems overkill). Triple quotes seem unlikely in most cases but might also be worth considering.

There's also a risk of variable name conflicts; if you have a local scope that reuses the global name for the constant, that will need some manual handling. Hopefully, you're choosing a global name that doesn't have that a problem.

Q: What is the point of a 16-bit wide character? A:

The original sin of Unicode was the Unicode Consortium believing that 16 bits would be enough forever, if they could only make Japanese and Chinese people accept that a single encoding for all of their languages was good enough.

Then, they belatedly decided that they needed round-trip compatibility with every entity in every other character set that has ever been used, including a bunch of dingbat and emoji fonts. And that meant they needed room for tens of thousands more. But by then, Microsoft Windows had made 16-bit Unicode part of its operating system, and it was set in stone. So, UTF-8 and UTF-16 were both invented for backward-compatibility with an existing encoding, and UTF-8 is a lot more practical.

You should consider UTF-16 obsolete. The one situation I can think of where I still need it is that the Windows GDI subsystem does not yet support different code pages for different processes, so a program might need to fall back on UTF-16 for some system calls, to run correctly on machines still configured to use 8-bit code pages.

Q: Is this Deep Learning → GenAI roadmap (project-based) sufficient for transitioning into LLM & GenAI engineering in 2026? A:

I know very little about the technology you are trying to learn. But I do know a bit about education (formal and workplace). So ...

Is this roadmap technically sound ...

There is no such thing as a "technically sound" educational roadmap. Sure, it is best if cover and understand the basics first, but you can always "backfill" any topics that you skipped (accidentally or deliberately) if you find that you need to.

Are there critical gaps ...

I can't see how any gap / missing step in a educational roadmap (at this level) could be a priori critical. (See previous.)

You shouldn't be aiming to learn everything. It is more efficient to learn what you will (or are likely to) need. And >we< can't reliably predict what that will be. The AI landscape is changing so quickly that I don't think anyone can reliably predict where it will be in even a couple of years.

Any ordering changes you would recommend based on real-world industry practice?

In real-world industry1, you do the tasks directed by your bosses, and (I bet) they wouldn't be able to reliably predict what skills you will need at any given time. (Even assuming that you knew who they will be and could ask them.)

My advice: just get on with it. Trust your own judgement, and learn from your mistakes.

People who confidently predict the future of AI are either delusional or con artists. IMO.

1 - Is there any other kind of industry?
